intervention_evidence: Neumark and Stock 2006, The Labor Market Effects of Sex and Race Discrimination Laws, Economic Inquiry | Roy 2019, Discriminatory Laws Against Women: A Survey of the Literature, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 8719
finding: In the US, state equal-pay laws lowered women's relative employment, while race discrimination laws showed some evidence of raising Black relative earnings; a World Bank survey finds legal gender discrimination harms women's outcomes, though evidence comes mostly from developed countries.
basis: Neumark abstract: equal-pay laws cut relative female employment, race laws some earnings gain; Roy abstract: negative effects of discriminatory laws, evidence mostly developed countries.

intervention_evidence: Halim, Perova and Reynolds 2023, Childcare and Mothers' Labor Market Outcomes in Lower- and Middle-Income Countries, World Bank Research Observer
finding: Across 22 credible studies in lower- and middle-income countries, nearly all find that institutional childcare raises mothers' employment or hours of work; gains may depend on design, such as hours of care, children's ages and coordination with other care.
basis: abstract: review of 22 causal studies, nearly all positive effects on maternal work; discusses hours, child age and coordination as design factors.

intervention_evidence: Betcherman 2015, Labor Market Regulations: What Do We Know about Their Impacts in Developing Countries?, World Bank Research Observer
finding: In developing countries, minimum wages and employment protection usually have modest effects on employment, earnings and productivity, sometimes in either direction; covered workers gain some equalisation, while youth, women and less-skilled workers are disproportionately left outside coverage.
basis: abstract (narrative review): modest effects of minimum wages and EPL, either direction; distributional effects favour covered workers, exclude youth, women, less-skilled.

intervention_evidence: Jessen and Kluve 2021, The effectiveness of interventions to reduce informality in low- and middle-income countries, World Development
finding: Across 38 studies in low- and middle-income countries, tax incentives are the most effective formalisation tool and information campaigns help as complements; large-scale policies outperform single programmes, and effects are larger for worker registration and in favourable labour markets.
basis: abstract: meta-analysis of 170 estimates from 38 studies; tax incentives especially effective, information complements, large-scale better, better labour markets help.

intervention_evidence: OECD 2019, Negotiating Our Way Up: Collective Bargaining in a Changing World of Work, OECD Publishing
finding: In OECD countries, coordinated systems where sectoral agreements set broad conditions and leave details to firm bargaining show the best employment, productivity and wage outcomes; agreement coverage has fallen and non-standard workers are much less often unionised.
basis: OECD launch summary (reposted): best outcomes with coordinated sectoral-plus-firm bargaining; coverage fell from 46% to 32%; non-standard workers 50% less likely unionised. Full report not reached.

intervention_evidence: Mischke et al. 2013, Occupational safety and health enforcement tools for preventing occupational diseases and injuries, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
finding: Workplace inspections showed no short-term injury reduction in a randomised trial, while controlled before-after studies suggest fewer injuries over the medium and long term; all of this evidence is of low quality.
basis: Cochrane summary-of-findings table: RCT short-term RR 1.04; controlled before-after medium RR 0.87, long-term RR 0.77; low-quality evidence.

intervention_evidence: Banerjee, Finkelstein, Hanna, Olken, Ornaghi and Sumarto 2021, The Challenges of Universal Health Insurance in Developing Countries: Experimental Evidence from Indonesia's National Health Insurance, American Economic Review
finding: In an experiment with about 6,000 Indonesian households, time-limited premium subsidies raised enrolment in national health insurance and drew in lower-cost enrollees; registration help raised attempts, but over half of attempts failed, showing weak administrative capacity limits coverage.
basis: abstract: randomised subsidies raised enrolment and attracted lower-cost enrollees; assistance raised attempted enrolment, more than half failed; weak state capacity.

intervention_evidence: Saran, White and Kuper 2020, Evidence and gap map of studies assessing the effectiveness of interventions for people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries, Campbell Systematic Reviews
finding: An evidence map of 166 studies on people with disabilities in low- and middle-income countries finds most concern health and rehabilitation, very few measure access to assistive devices, and study quality is a significant gap.
basis: abstract: 166 studies, 118 on health; very few measure assistive-device access; empowerment virtually none; significant gap in study quality.

intervention_evidence: Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2016, Building State Capacity: Evidence from Biometric Smartcards in India, American Economic Review | Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2025, Identity Verification Standards in Welfare Programs: Experimental Evidence from India, Review of Economics and Statistics
finding: In Andhra Pradesh, biometric smartcards made welfare payments faster, more predictable and less corrupt without reducing access; stricter biometric checks in India's largest social protection programme cut corruption but cost 1.5-2 million genuine beneficiaries their benefits at some point.
basis: 2016 abstract: randomised rollout, faster, less corrupt payments, access unchanged; 2025 abstract: corruption fell, 1.5-2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access, mainly from transition management.

intervention_evidence: Field, Pande, Rigol, Schaner and Troyer Moore 2021, On Her Own Account: How Strengthening Women's Financial Control Impacts Labor Supply and Gender Norms, American Economic Review
finding: In rural India, paying women's public-sector wages into their own bank accounts, with training, raised their work in public and private jobs and, three years later, liberalised their own and perceived community norms about women working.
basis: abstract: randomised direct deposit plus training increased women's work versus accounts only; three years later women's work norms and perceived community norms liberalised.

intervention_evidence: Beaman, Chattopadhyay, Duflo, Pande and Topalova 2009, Powerful Women: Does Exposure Reduce Bias?, Quarterly Journal of Economics
finding: Randomly assigned quotas for women heads of Indian village councils improved voters' views of female leaders' effectiveness and weakened gender stereotypes; after ten years, women were more likely to stand and win where seats had been reserved twice.
basis: abstract: random assignment of quotas; prior exposure improves perceived effectiveness, weakens stereotypes; women more likely to stand and win after two reserved cycles.

intervention_evidence: Bagde, Epple and Taylor 2016, Does Affirmative Action Work? Caste, Gender, College Quality, and Academic Success in India, American Economic Review
finding: Caste and gender admission quotas at over 200 Indian engineering colleges raised attendance of targeted students, especially at higher-quality colleges, with no evidence that beneficiaries were harmed by placement in programmes they were unprepared for.
basis: abstract: quota policy increases college attendance of targeted students, particularly at better colleges; no evidence of harm from mismatch.

intervention_evidence: Buller, Peterman, Ranganathan, Bleile, Hidrobo and Heise 2018, A Mixed-Method Review of Cash Transfers and Intimate Partner Violence in Low- and Middle-Income Countries, World Bank Research Observer
finding: Across 14 quantitative and 8 qualitative studies in low- and middle-income countries, most found cash transfers reduced intimate partner violence and few found increases; programme design and complementary activities likely shape benefits and harms.
basis: abstract: 14 quantitative, 8 qualitative studies; most show IPV reductions, few increases; design and complementary activities matter.

intervention_evidence: Dammert, de Hoop, Mvukiyehe and Rosati 2018, Effects of public policy on child labor: Current knowledge, gaps, and implications for program design, World Development
finding: Across 33 impact evaluations, cash transfers reduced child labour in most cases and health insurance reduced reliance on it, but programmes that raise adults' labour market or business activity can increase children's work.
basis: abstract: 33 evaluations; transfers reduced child labour in most cases; policies raising adult labour or entrepreneurship may increase child work.

intervention_evidence: Buchmann, Field, Glennerster, Nazneen and Wang 2023, A Signal to End Child Marriage: Theory and Experimental Evidence from Bangladesh, American Economic Review | UNICEF 2021, Child Marriage Evidence Summary, UNICEF
finding: In Bangladesh, an incentive to delay marriage cut underage marriage among eligible girls by 19 percent, while an empowerment programme did not; a 2021 evidence summary finds school-support transfers most consistently delay marriage and minimum-age laws show little effect.
basis: Buchmann abstract: incentive 19 percent less underage marriage, empowerment no effect; UNICEF summary: school-support transfers 5 of 5 positive, little relation with legislation.

intervention_evidence: Cluver et al. 2018, Parenting for Lifelong Health: a pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial of a non-commercialised parenting programme for adolescents and their families in South Africa, BMJ Global Health
finding: A 14-session parenting programme in South Africa's Eastern Cape reduced caregiver-reported abuse and corporal punishment and improved parental supervision, though adolescents reported no significant reduction in abuse.
basis: abstract: cluster RCT, 552 families; caregivers reported less abuse and corporal punishment, adolescents did not; supervision improved; neglect unchanged.

intervention_evidence: Operations Evaluation Department 1993, Early Experience with Involuntary Resettlement: Overview, World Bank
finding: In four Bank-financed resettlement projects, incomes rose in Thailand and for about half of families in Maharashtra, but fell in Ghana and for Karnataka households losing house and land; government commitment, strong agencies, planning and income programmes underpinned success.
basis: report text: project-by-project income outcomes (Thailand up, Maharashtra half, Ghana down, Karnataka mixed); government commitment plus six factors explain satisfactory outcomes.

intervention_evidence: Bryan, Chowdhury and Mobarak 2014, Underinvestment in a Profitable Technology: The Case of Seasonal Migration in Bangladesh, Econometrica
finding: In rural Bangladesh, a small randomised incentive led about 22 percent of households to send a seasonal migrant, significantly raised consumption at home, and made households more likely to migrate again one and three years later.
basis: abstract: incentive offer, 22% sent a migrant, consumption rose significantly, 8-10 points more likely to re-migrate after one and three years.

intervention_evidence: Marbach, Hainmueller and Hangartner 2018, The long-term impact of employment bans on the economic integration of refugees, Science Advances | Clemens, Huang and Graham 2018, The Economic and Fiscal Effects of Granting Refugees Formal Labor Market Access, Center for Global Development Working Paper
finding: In Germany, refugees facing about seven months' longer employment bans had markedly lower employment years later, a gap taking up to ten years to close; a policy review argues work rights can benefit refugees and hosts, with possible costs for some native groups.
basis: Marbach abstract: court-ruling natural experiment, employment about 20 points lower after five years; Clemens abstract: argument paper on potential benefits, possible costs for some natives.

intervention_evidence: Carter, de Janvry, Sadoulet and Sarris 2017, Index Insurance for Developing Country Agriculture: A Reassessment, Annual Review of Resource Economics | Janzen and Carter 2019, After the Drought: The Impact of Microinsurance on Consumption Smoothing and Asset Protection, American Journal of Agricultural Economics
finding: In a Kenyan experiment, livestock microinsurance reduced asset sales by wealthier households and meal-cutting by poorer ones after drought; across developing countries, take-up of index insurance has been disappointingly low without large, sustained subsidies.
basis: Janzen-Carter abstract: RCT, insurance reduces both costly coping strategies; Carter et al. abstract: take-up disappointingly low without large sustained subsidies.

intervention_evidence: Pople, Hill, Dercon and Brunckhorst 2021, Anticipatory Cash Transfers in Climate Disaster Response, CSAE Working Paper
finding: Cash paid to Bangladeshi households ahead of forecast extreme floods cut the chance of going a day without eating during the flood and, three months on, improved food consumption and wellbeing and reduced asset losses and costly borrowing.
basis: abstract: recipients versus similar non-recipients; 36% less likely to go a day without eating; later better food consumption, wellbeing, lower asset losses and costly borrowing.

intervention_evidence: Galiani, Gertler and Bando 2016, Non-contributory pensions, Labour Economics | Duflo 2003, Grandmothers and Granddaughters: Old-Age Pensions and Intrahousehold Allocation in South Africa, World Bank Economic Review
finding: Mexico's rural non-contributory pension for people over 70 raised household consumption, lowered depression scores and reduced paid work; in South Africa, pensions received by women improved granddaughters' growth, while pensions received by men did not.
basis: Galiani abstract: age and geographic cutoffs; consumption up, depression down, paid work down; Duflo abstract: women's pensions improved girls' anthropometrics, men's no effect.

intervention_evidence: Erlangga, Suhrcke, Ali and Bloor 2019, The impact of public health insurance on health care utilisation, financial protection and health status in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review, PLoS ONE
finding: Across 68 studies in low- and middle-income countries, public health insurance raised facility use in 32 of 40 studies and improved financial protection in 26 of 46, with moderate evidence of better health; results are not fully consistent.
basis: abstract: 68 studies; access improved 32/40, financial protection 26/46, health 9/12; authors note findings not entirely consistent.

intervention_evidence: Alatas, Banerjee, Hanna, Olken, Purnamasari and Wai-Poi 2016, Self-Targeting: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Indonesia, Journal of Political Economy
finding: In an Indonesian village experiment, requiring households to apply produced substantially poorer beneficiaries than automatic enrolment under the same asset test, mainly because non-poor households did not apply; raising application costs further did not improve targeting.
basis: abstract: application requirement yields poorer beneficiaries than automatic enrolment; higher costs no further gain; driven by non-poor not applying.

intervention_evidence: Bastagli et al. 2016, Cash transfers: what does the evidence say? A rigorous review of programme impact and of the role of design and implementation features, ODI | Pega et al. 2022, Unconditional cash transfers for reducing poverty and vulnerabilities: effect on use of health services and health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
finding: In low- and middle-income countries, unconditional transfers probably reduce illness and raise school attendance and may reduce extreme poverty; a wider review finds strong evidence that cash transfers cut poverty, with larger transfers more likely to achieve intended effects.
basis: Cochrane SoF: illness and attendance moderate certainty, extreme poverty low; ODI briefing: strong evidence of poverty reduction, higher transfer levels linked to intended effects.

intervention_evidence: Banerjee, Duflo and Sharma 2021, Long-Term Effects of the Targeting the Ultra Poor Program, American Economic Review: Insights | Bossuroy et al. 2022, Tackling psychosocial and capital constraints to alleviate poverty, Nature
finding: In India, a graduation programme's asset transfer raised consumption, food security, income and health for ten years, partly through migration into wage work; in Niger, coaching and savings groups plus cash or psychosocial support all helped, psychosocial arms being most cost-effective.
basis: Banerjee abstract: ten-year RCT, gains grew seven years and persisted; Bossuroy summary: all three arms improved outcomes, psychosocial arms most cost-effective.

intervention_evidence: Baird, Ferreira, Ozler and Woolcock 2014, Conditional, unconditional and everything in between: a systematic review of the effects of cash transfer programmes on schooling outcomes, Journal of Development Effectiveness
finding: Both conditional and unconditional transfers raise enrolment and attendance; explicitly monitored and enforced conditions produce larger schooling gains, while learning effects are small.
basis: abstract: 35 studies; CCTs and UCTs raise enrolment and attendance; explicit, monitored, enforced conditions give larger enrolment effects; test-score effects small at best.

intervention_evidence: Hidrobo, Hoddinott, Kumar and Olivier 2018, Social Protection, Food Security, and Asset Formation, World Development | Jensen and Miller 2011, Do Consumer Price Subsidies Really Improve Nutrition?, Review of Economics and Statistics
finding: A meta-analysis finds social protection raises the quantity and quality of food consumed, with food spending rising more than calories as diets shift to animal-source foods; randomised staple price subsidies in two Chinese provinces showed no evidence of better nutrition.
basis: Hidrobo abstract: food expenditure up 13%, calories 8%, animal-source shift; Jensen-Miller abstract: randomised subsidies, no evidence nutrition improved, possibly harmed some.

intervention_evidence: Bhutta et al. 2013, Evidence-based interventions for improvement of maternal and child nutrition: what can be done and at what cost?, The Lancet
finding: Modelling for 34 high-burden countries estimates that ten proven nutrition interventions at 90 percent coverage would cut under-five deaths by about 15 percent at about Int$9.6 billion a year; linking them to nutrition-sensitive programmes could speed progress.
basis: abstract: updated evidence review plus model in 34 countries; ten interventions at 90% coverage, about 15% fewer under-5 deaths, Int$9.6 billion yearly.

intervention_evidence: Hoffmann, Moser and Saak 2019, Food safety in low and middle-income countries: The evidence through an economic lens, World Development
finding: A review of evidence from low- and middle-income countries traces unsafe food to limited consumer awareness and ability to pay, weak incentives for firms and farmers, and weak public enforcement; co-regulation with mid-size and large firms and rewards for safety investment look promising.
basis: abstract (narrative review): three contributors to food safety problems; co-regulation and rewarding safety investment named as promising; no impact estimates.

intervention_evidence: Omotilewa, Ricker-Gilbert, Ainembabazi and Shively 2018, Does improved storage technology promote modern input use and food security? Evidence from a randomized trial in Uganda, Journal of Development Economics | Burke, Bergquist and Miguel 2019, Sell Low and Buy High: Arbitrage and Local Price Effects in Kenyan Markets, Quarterly Journal of Economics
finding: In a Ugandan trial, improved storage technology sharply cut storage losses, lengthened storage and raised hybrid maize planting; in Kenya, timely harvest loans let farmers store and sell later at high returns, with local price effects depending on loan density.
basis: Omotilewa abstract: RCT of 1,200 farmers, lower losses, longer storage, 10 points more hybrid planting; Burke abstract: loans gave 29% return, general-equilibrium price effects.

intervention_evidence: Wang, Shinde, Young and Fawzi 2021, Impacts of school feeding on educational and health outcomes of school-age children and adolescents in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Journal of Global Health
finding: Across 57 studies in low- and middle-income countries, school feeding raised attendance and modestly increased height and weight over a year; effects on nutrition and academic achievement still need confirmation from better-designed research.
basis: abstract: 44 RCTs and 13 controlled studies; pooled attendance +2.6 points, height +0.32 cm, weight +0.58 kg; more research needed on nutrition and achievement.

intervention_evidence: Braga, Turchan, Papachristos and Hureau 2019, Hot spots policing and crime reduction: an update of an ongoing systematic review and meta-analysis, Journal of Experimental Criminology | Blair et al. 2021, Community policing does not build citizen trust in police or reduce crime in the Global South, Science
finding: Hot spots policing reduces crime, with benefits diffusing to nearby areas rather than displacing crime; but coordinated community policing trials in Brazil, Colombia, Liberia, Pakistan, the Philippines and Uganda found no fall in crime or better citizen-police relations.
basis: Braga abstract: robust evidence of crime prevention, diffusion not displacement; Blair abstract: six field experiments, preregistered meta-analysis, no crime reduction, relations not improved.

intervention_evidence: Blattman, Chaskel, Jamison and Sheridan 2023, Cognitive Behavior Therapy Reduces Crime and Violence over Ten Years: Experimental Evidence, American Economic Review: Insights
finding: In Liberia, eight weeks of cognitive behavioural therapy for high-risk men roughly halved antisocial behaviours such as robbery and drug selling ten years later, with effects concentrated among the highest-risk men and most robust when combined with cash.
basis: abstract: 999 men randomised to therapy, cash, both or neither; therapy groups about half as likely to engage in antisocial behaviour after ten years.

intervention_evidence: Anda, Hammaker, Khan, Sonnenfeld and Glandon 2022, Evidence Gap Map Practitioner Brief: Service-Level Rule of Law Interventions, 3ie | Chemin 2009, The impact of the judiciary on entrepreneurship: Evaluation of Pakistan's Access to Justice Programme, Journal of Public Economics
finding: Few evaluations exist: in Liberia and Haiti free legal aid improved perceived outcomes and cut illegal pretrial detention, while paralegal programmes changed knowledge more than behaviour; a Pakistani judicial reform raised case disposal and new firm entry.
basis: 3ie brief: about eight evaluations, legal aid effects in Kenya, Liberia, Haiti, paralegals mixed in Liberia and Tanzania; Chemin abstract: quarter more cases disposed, firm entry up.

intervention_evidence: Di Tella and Schargrodsky 2013, Criminal Recidivism after Prison and Electronic Monitoring, Journal of Political Economy | Lipsey, Landenberger and Wilson 2007, Effects of cognitive-behavioral programs for criminal offenders, Campbell Systematic Reviews
finding: In Argentina, electronic monitoring instead of prison substantially reduced re-arrest; a Campbell review finds cognitive behavioural programmes reduce reoffending, most when well implemented by trained providers, with no difference between programme brands or prison and community settings.
basis: Di Tella abstract: random judge assignment, large negative effect of monitoring on recidivism; Lipsey abstract: CBT effective, varies with implementation quality, not brand or setting.

intervention_evidence: Werb et al. 2011, Effect of drug law enforcement on drug market violence: A systematic review, International Journal of Drug Policy | Castillo, Mejia and Restrepo 2020, Scarcity without Leviathan: The Violent Effects of Cocaine Supply Shortages in the Mexican Drug War, Review of Economics and Statistics
finding: Fourteen of the reviewed studies (93 percent) found drug law enforcement increased market violence, and the review judges more enforcement unlikely to reduce it; in Mexico, cocaine scarcity from Colombian seizures raised violence, most where several cartels operated.
basis: Werb abstract: 93% of studies report adverse effect of enforcement on violence; Castillo abstract: seizure-driven scarcity raised Mexican violence, larger with multiple cartels.

intervention_evidence: Independent Evaluation Group 2008, The Welfare Impact of Rural Electrification: A Reassessment of the Costs and Benefits, World Bank | Lee, Miguel and Wolfram 2020, Experimental Evidence on the Economics of Rural Electrification, Journal of Political Economy
finding: A World Bank evaluation finds rural households value electricity for lighting, study and television, with willingness to pay above long-run supply cost; but a Kenyan grid experiment found little electricity use and no meaningful medium-run economic or non-economic effects.
basis: IEG abstract: benefits from lighting, study, TV; willingness to pay exceeds long-run marginal cost; Lee abstract: randomised connections, low use, no meaningful medium-run effects.

intervention_evidence: Kremer, Luby, Maertens, Tan and Wiecek 2023, Water Treatment and Child Mortality: A Meta-Analysis and Cost-effectiveness Analysis, NBER Working Paper
finding: Pooling 18 trials in low- and middle-income countries, household water treatment cut the odds of under-five death by about 24 to 27 percent, making it one of the most cost-effective health programmes; this source does not assess sanitation.
basis: abstract: 18 studies from 52 trials; all-cause under-5 mortality odds reduced about 24-27%; USD 28-72 per DALY averted.

intervention_evidence: Clasen et al. 2022, Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass for Cooking and Effects on Birth Weight, New England Journal of Medicine | Berkouwer and Dean 2022, Credit, Attention, and Externalities in the Adoption of Energy Efficient Technologies by Low-Income Households, American Economic Review
finding: In Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda, free LPG stoves and fuel nearly eliminated biomass use and cut pollution exposure but did not change birth weight; in Nairobi, efficient charcoal stoves cut charcoal spending, and loans more than doubled willingness to pay.
basis: Clasen abstract: 3,200 women randomised, low biomass use, lower PM2.5, no significant birth-weight difference; Berkouwer abstract: 39% less charcoal spending, credit doubled demand.

intervention_evidence: Turley, Saith, Bhan, Rehfuess and Carter 2013, Slum upgrading strategies involving physical environment and infrastructure interventions and their effects on health and socio-economic outcomes, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Barnhardt, Field and Pande 2017, Moving to Opportunity or Isolation? Network Effects of a Randomized Housing Lottery in Urban India, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics
finding: Limited but consistent evidence suggests slum upgrading may reduce diarrhoea and water spending, with inconsistent effects on poverty and jobs; in an Indian housing lottery, winners got better peripheral housing but no income gain and lost family and caste networks.
basis: Cochrane summary: five main studies, limited consistent evidence on diarrhoea and water costs; Barnhardt abstract: better housing, no income change, isolation, a third later left.

intervention_evidence: Rocha and Soares 2010, Evaluating the impact of community-based health interventions: evidence from Brazil's Family Health Program, Health Economics | Gruber, Hendren and Townsend 2014, The Great Equalizer: Health Care Access and Infant Mortality in Thailand, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics
finding: Brazil's Family Health Program reduced mortality, mostly among the young, with wider gains in the poorest regions; Thailand's reform raising hospital funding for the poor and cutting copays increased care use and erased the infant mortality gap between poor and rich provinces.
basis: Rocha-Soares abstract: mortality reduced, labour supply and enrolment up in poorest regions; Gruber abstract: use rose, infant mortality fell, poor-rich gap disappears.

intervention_evidence: Rowe et al. 2018, Effectiveness of strategies to improve health-care provider practices in low-income and middle-income countries: a systematic review, The Lancet Global Health | Basinga et al. 2011, Effect on maternal and child health services in Rwanda of payment to primary health-care providers for performance: an impact evaluation, The Lancet
finding: In low- and middle-income countries, group problem solving improved provider practices most, followed by combined training and supervision, with large variation; in Rwanda, performance pay raised institutional deliveries and preventive visits but not prenatal visit completion or full immunisation.
basis: Rowe summary: training or supervision alone about 10-16 points, combined about 18, group problem solving 28-38; Basinga abstract: RCT, deliveries up 23%, no immunisation gain.

intervention_evidence: Lewin et al. 2010, Lay health workers in primary and community health care for maternal and child health and the management of infectious diseases, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Grobler et al. 2015, Interventions for increasing the proportion of health professionals practising in rural and other underserved areas, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
finding: Lay health workers raised immunisation uptake, breastfeeding and tuberculosis cure rates in 82 trials, mostly from high-income countries; for keeping professionals in rural and underserved areas, a Cochrane review found only one eligible study and very low-certainty evidence.
basis: Lewin abstract: 82 RCTs, gains in immunisation, breastfeeding, TB cure; Grobler summary: one interrupted time series from Taiwan, very low certainty.

intervention_evidence: Acosta et al. 2014, Pharmaceutical policies: effects of reference pricing, other pricing, and purchasing policies, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Bjorkman Nyqvist, Svensson and Yanagizawa-Drott 2022, Can Good Products Drive Out Bad? A Randomized Intervention in the Antimalarial Medicine Market in Uganda, Journal of the European Economic Association
finding: Reference pricing lowered insurers' drug spending in a few low-quality studies, none of which measured health effects; in Uganda, entry of an NGO selling authentic antimalarials below market price more than halved the share of local outlets selling fake drugs.
basis: Cochrane SoF: reference pricing cut insurer drug spending, low-quality evidence, no studies on health outcomes; Bjorkman Nyqvist abstract: RCT, fake-drug sellers down over 50%.

intervention_evidence: Lassi and Bhutta 2015, Community-based intervention packages for reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality and improving neonatal outcomes, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Banerjee, Duflo, Glennerster and Kothari 2010, Improving immunisation coverage in rural India: clustered randomised controlled evaluation of immunisation campaigns with and without incentives, BMJ
finding: Community-based maternal and newborn packages reduced neonatal and perinatal mortality and stillbirths, with no significant effect on maternal mortality; in rural Rajasthan, reliable immunisation camps raised full immunisation modestly, and adding small incentives raised it far more.
basis: Lassi pooled analyses: neonatal mortality RR 0.75 across 21 studies, maternal mortality CI includes 1; Banerjee abstract: full immunisation 39% with incentives, 18% camps, 6% control.

intervention_evidence: Teng et al. 2019, Impact of sugar-sweetened beverage taxes on purchases and dietary intake: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Obesity Reviews | Colchero et al. 2016, Beverage purchases from stores in Mexico under the excise tax on sugar sweetened beverages: observational study, BMJ
finding: Across sugary drink taxes in US cities, Catalonia, Chile, France and Mexico, a 10 percent tax cut purchases by about 10 percent; in Mexico, purchases of taxed drinks fell after the tax, most among low-income households.
basis: Teng: university summary of the meta-analysis, about 10% volume fall per 10% tax; Colchero abstract: difference-in-differences, taxed purchases down 6% in 2014, low-SES 9%.

intervention_evidence: Pryce, Richardson and Lengeler 2018, Insecticide-treated nets for preventing malaria, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Cohen and Dupas 2010, Free Distribution or Cost-Sharing? Evidence from a Randomized Malaria Prevention Experiment, Quarterly Journal of Economics
finding: Insecticide-treated nets reduce all-cause child mortality and severe malaria compared with no nets; in Kenya, free nets given to pregnant women were used as much as subsidised ones, while small prices sharply cut uptake.
basis: Cochrane summary: 17% lower child mortality, high certainty; Cohen-Dupas abstract: free nets no less used, uptake fell 75% from zero to USD 0.75.

intervention_evidence: Chaloupka, Yurekli and Fong 2012, Tobacco taxes as a tobacco control strategy, Tobacco Control | Wagenaar, Salois and Komro 2009, Effects of beverage alcohol price and tax levels on drinking: a meta-analysis of 1003 estimates from 112 studies, Addiction
finding: Over 100 studies, including from low- and middle-income countries, show tobacco tax increases cut use, most among young and poor people; a meta-analysis of 112 studies finds higher alcohol prices significantly reduce drinking of beer, wine and spirits.
basis: Chaloupka abstract: over 100 studies, taxes reduce use, largest effect on young and poor; Wagenaar abstract: mean elasticities beer -0.46, wine -0.69, spirits -0.80, highly significant.

intervention_evidence: Staton et al. 2016, Road Traffic Injury Prevention Initiatives: A Systematic Review and Metasummary of Effectiveness in Low and Middle Income Countries, PLoS ONE | Liu et al. 2008, Helmets for preventing injury in motorcycle riders, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
finding: In 18 studies from 11 low- and middle-income countries, road safety legislation worked best with strong enforcement or as part of multifaceted programmes; wearing a motorcycle helmet cuts the risk of death by about 42 percent and head injury by about 69 percent.
basis: Staton abstract: 18 studies, legislation best with strong enforcement or multifaceted approach; Liu Cochrane summary: helmets OR 0.58 death, OR 0.31 head injury.

intervention_evidence: Barbui et al. 2020, Efficacy of psychosocial interventions for mental health outcomes in low-income and middle-income countries: an umbrella review, The Lancet Psychiatry
finding: An umbrella review of 123 trials in low- and middle-income countries finds psychosocial interventions benefit many mental health outcomes, with the strongest evidence for adults with depression in humanitarian settings and common mental disorders; strength varies by condition and setting.
basis: abstract: 123 studies in ten reviews; highly suggestive evidence for depression in humanitarian settings (SMD 0.87) and common mental disorders (0.49); variation by condition.

intervention_evidence: Burde and Linden 2013, Bringing Education to Afghan Girls: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Village-Based Schools, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics | Petrosino et al. 2012, Interventions in Developing Nations for Improving Primary and Secondary School Enrollment of Children: A Systematic Review, Campbell Systematic Reviews
finding: Village-based schools in rural Afghanistan raised enrolment and test scores, most for girls, closing the gender gap in enrolment; across 73 studies, interventions to get and keep children in school have small positive average effects with large variation.
basis: Burde abstract: RCT, girls' enrolment up 52 points, scores up 0.65 SD; Petrosino abstract: 73 studies, positive average effects of 3-9%, significant heterogeneity.

intervention_evidence: Evans and Popova 2016, What Really Works to Improve Learning in Developing Countries? An Analysis of Divergent Findings in Systematic Reviews, World Bank Research Observer | Banerjee et al. 2017, From Proof of Concept to Scalable Policies: Challenges and Solutions, with an Application, Journal of Economic Perspectives
finding: Learning reviews most consistently support teaching matched to children's learning levels and repeated teacher training tied to specific tasks; in India, scaling Teaching at the Right Level in government schools failed in early designs, but two versions raised learning.
basis: Evans-Popova abstract: consistent recommendations for level-targeted pedagogy and task-specific training; Banerjee abstract: early government designs failed, two later versions raised learning at scale.

intervention_evidence: Popova, Evans, Breeding and Arancibia 2022, Teacher Professional Development around the World: The Gap between Evidence and Practice, World Bank Research Observer | de Ree, Muralidharan, Pradhan and Rogers 2018, Double for Nothing? Experimental Evidence on an Unconditional Teacher Salary Increase in Indonesia, Quarterly Journal of Economics
finding: Across 33 evaluated programmes, teacher training with career incentives, subject focus, practice and initial face-to-face sessions brings larger learning gains, features most at-scale programmes lack; doubling Indonesian teachers' pay unconditionally raised satisfaction but not student learning.
basis: Popova abstract: 33 programmes, listed features linked to larger gains, 139 at-scale programmes lack them; de Ree abstract: RCT, satisfaction up, no learning gain.

intervention_evidence: Britto et al. 2017, Nurturing care: promoting early childhood development, The Lancet | Gertler et al. 2014, Labor market returns to an early childhood stimulation intervention in Jamaica, Science
finding: A Lancet review concludes early childhood interventions work best as multi-sectoral packages built on nurturing care and caregiver support; in Jamaica, two years of weekly home visits for stunted toddlers substantially raised their earnings twenty years later.
basis: Britto abstract: multi-sectoral packages anchored in nurturing care; Gertler working-paper abstract: randomised home visits, earnings raised 20 years later (Science version via summary page).

intervention_evidence: Lucas and Mbiti 2012, Access, Sorting, and Achievement: The Short-Run Effects of Free Primary Education in Kenya, American Economic Journal: Applied Economics | Kremer, Miguel and Thornton 2009, Incentives to Learn, Review of Economics and Statistics
finding: Kenya's free primary education raised completion and access for disadvantaged pupils without substantially lowering others' scores; a randomised girls' merit scholarship in Kenya raised exam scores, including for low-scoring girls unlikely to win, though results in one district were unclear.
basis: Lucas-Mbiti abstract: completion and disadvantaged access up, scores not substantially lower; Kremer abstract: scores up, spillovers to low scorers, one district inconclusive from attrition.

intervention_evidence: Taylor-Robinson et al. 2019, Public health deworming programmes for soil-transmitted helminths in children living in endemic areas, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | Freeman et al. 2012, Assessing the impact of a school-based water treatment, hygiene and sanitation programme on pupil absence in Nyanza Province, Kenya: a cluster-randomized trial, Tropical Medicine and International Health
finding: Regular school-age deworming shows little or no effect on height, haemoglobin, cognition, school performance or mortality, with inconsistent attendance evidence; in Kenya, school water treatment and hygiene cut girls' absence only in areas unaffected by post-election violence.
basis: Cochrane abstract: 51 trials, little or no effect, attendance evidence inconsistent; Freeman abstract: no overall effect, girls' absence odds down 58% in two areas.

intervention_evidence: Ferreyra, Avitabile, Botero Alvarez, Haimovich Paz and Urzua 2017, At a Crossroads: Higher Education in Latin America and the Caribbean, World Bank | Hastings, Neilson and Zimmerman 2013, Are Some Degrees Worth More than Others? Evidence from College Admission Cutoffs in Chile, NBER Working Paper
finding: Higher education in Latin America has expanded sharply since 2000, with more equitable access but persistent quality concerns; in Chile, returns vary widely, with large gains for selective and health, science and social science degrees regardless of socioeconomic status.
basis: Ferreyra abstract: expansion since 2000, access more equitable, quality concerns; Hastings abstract: regression discontinuity, heterogeneous returns, no variation by SES.

intervention_evidence: McKenzie 2017, How Effective Are Active Labor Market Policies in Developing Countries? A Critical Review of Recent Evidence, World Bank Research Observer | Kluve, Puerto, Robalino, Romero, Rother, Stoterau, Weidenkaff and Witte 2019, Do youth employment programs improve labor market outcomes? A quantitative review, World Development
finding: Recent developing-country evaluations of vocational training and other active labour market programmes often find no significant employment or earnings effects; across 113 youth programme evaluations worldwide, average effects are small, larger in low and middle income countries and where design and delivery are strong.
basis: McKenzie abstract: many evaluations, including vocational training, find no significant impacts; Kluve abstract: small pooled effects, larger in LMICs, design matters more than type.

intervention_evidence: Alfonsi, Bandiera, Bassi, Burgess, Rasul, Sulaiman and Vitali 2020, Tackling Youth Unemployment: Evidence from a Labor Market Experiment in Uganda, Econometrica
finding: In Uganda, six months of firm-provided training and of certified vocational training both improved youth employment; firm-training gains came fast but faded, while vocational gains lasted because certified skills brought more job offers.
basis: Abstract: experiment with 1,700 workers and 1,500 firms; firm-training gains fade, vocational gains last; more job offers attributed to verifiable certified skills.

intervention_evidence: Carranza, Garlick, Orkin and Rankin 2022, Job Search and Hiring with Limited Information about Workseekers' Skills, American Economic Review
finding: Giving South African workseekers skill assessment results they could credibly show employers raised employment and earnings; results employers could not verify shifted beliefs and search but had smaller labour market effects.
basis: Abstract: credible, shareable assessments raise employment and earnings; non-verifiable ones have smaller effects; sharing only with employers changes interview decisions.

intervention_evidence: Novella, Freund and Rosas-Shady 2026, Digital skills for better jobs: Experimental evidence from a bootcamp training program in Peru, Journal of Development Economics
finding: An online digital skills bootcamp for Peruvian youth raised entry into entry-level technology jobs two years on, but average effects on formal employment and income were null because only some course tracks paid off, possibly reflecting limited local demand.
basis: Abstract: randomized evaluation with administrative data; tech-job entry rises; some tracks positive, others null; selection and limited local demand suggested as reasons.

intervention_evidence: Hjort and Poulsen 2019, The Arrival of Fast Internet and Employment in Africa, American Economic Review | Cristia, Ibarraran, Cueto, Santiago and Severin 2017, Technology and Child Development: Evidence from the One Laptop per Child Program, AEJ: Applied Economics
finding: Arrival of fast internet in African countries raised employment rates, mainly in higher-skilled jobs, with little displacement; in contrast, giving laptops to rural Peruvian pupils raised computer use but had no effect on maths or language scores.
basis: Hjort abstract: submarine-cable arrival raises employment, mostly skilled, little displacement; Cristia abstract: RCT in 318 schools, more computer use, no test-score effects.

intervention_evidence: Dobbeling-Hildebrandt et al. 2024, Systematic review and meta-analysis of ex-post evaluations on the effectiveness of carbon pricing, Nature Communications
finding: Across 21 carbon pricing schemes evaluated ex post, introducing a price cut emissions by 5 to 21 percent where significant, about 10 percent on average, despite mostly low prices; China's pilot schemes showed larger cuts, and many schemes remain unevaluated.
basis: Abstract: 483 effect sizes from 80 causal evaluations; significant reductions of 5 to 21 percent; text: average 10.4 percent, Chinese pilots 13.1 percent.

intervention_evidence: Stechemesser et al. 2024, Climate policies that achieved major emission reductions: Global evidence from two decades, Science
finding: Of about 1,500 climate policies in 41 countries from 1998 to 2022, only 63 produced large emission breaks; price-based instruments played an important role within well-designed policy mixes, so clean-technology support works best combined with other instruments.
basis: Abstract: machine-learning difference-in-differences on 1,500 policies; 63 successful interventions; stresses price-based instruments in well-designed mixes.

intervention_evidence: Davis, Fuchs and Gertler 2014, Cash for Coolers: Evaluating a Large-Scale Appliance Replacement Program in Mexico, AEJ: Economic Policy | Fowlie, Greenstone and Wolfram 2018, Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program, QJE
finding: Subsidised efficiency upgrades saved less than projected: Mexico's refrigerator replacement cut use by about a quarter of predicted savings while air-conditioner replacement raised use, and Michigan weatherisation saved under a third of projected energy, with costs exceeding benefits.
basis: Davis abstract: fridges cut use 8 percent, a quarter of predictions, ACs raised use; Fowlie abstract: projected savings over three times actual, costs exceed benefits.

intervention_evidence: Fisch-Romito, Guivarch, Creutzig, Minx and Callaghan 2021, Systematic map of the literature on carbon lock-in induced by long-lived capital, Environmental Research Letters
finding: A systematic map of 226 publications finds the carbon lock-in literature biased towards power generation and developed countries and focused on committed emissions and stranded assets; it does not evaluate which planning or investment rules avoid lock-in.
basis: Abstract: 226 publications mapped; bias to electricity and developed countries; calls for research in developing countries and beyond power; no policy evaluation.

intervention_evidence: Rud, Simmons, Toews and Aragon 2024, Job displacement costs of phasing out coal, Journal of Public Economics | Hyman 2022, Can Displaced Labor Be Retrained? Evidence from Quasi-Random Assignment to Trade Adjustment Assistance, US Census Bureau CES Working Paper
finding: Displaced UK coal miners suffered large earnings losses still depressed fifteen years later; in the US, quasi-random approval for Trade Adjustment Assistance, which funds retraining, raised displaced workers' cumulative earnings over ten years, though annual gains faded.
basis: Rud abstract: wages fell 40 percent, losses persist fifteen years; Hyman abstract: TAA approval adds cumulative earnings, annual returns depreciate, effects tied to training.

intervention_evidence: Hino, Field and Orosco 2017, Managed retreat as a response to natural hazard risk, Nature Climate Change
finding: A review of 27 managed retreat cases, together resettling about 1.3 million people, finds drivers, barriers and outcomes differ by who benefits from relocation and who initiates it, with distinct sociopolitical factors decisive in each type.
basis: Abstract: 27 cases, 1.3 million resettled; conceptual model by beneficiary and initiator; different sociopolitical factors influential in each group.

intervention_evidence: Simmons, Czajkowski and Done 2018, Economic Effectiveness of Implementing a Statewide Building Code: The Case of Florida, Land Economics
finding: Florida's strict 2001 statewide building code, adopted after Hurricane Andrew, reduced insured windstorm losses by up to 72 percent, returning about six dollars in avoided losses per dollar of added cost with an eight-year payback.
basis: Abstract: ten years of paid insured loss data; losses reduced up to 72 percent; benefit-cost of 6 to 1; payback about 8 years.

intervention_evidence: Narayan et al. 2016, The Effectiveness, Costs and Coastal Protection Benefits of Natural and Nature-Based Defences, PLoS ONE
finding: Meta-analysis of 69 field measurements and 52 projects finds coastal habitats, especially coral reefs and salt marshes, substantially reduce wave heights, and salt marshes and mangroves can be two to five times cheaper than submerged breakwaters.
basis: Abstract: significant wave-height reduction potential; reefs and marshes highest; marshes and mangroves two to five times cheaper than submerged breakwaters.

intervention_evidence: Pittelkow et al. 2015, Productivity limits and potentials of the principles of conservation agriculture, Nature
finding: Global meta-analysis finds no-till contributes less to yields than often assumed; combined with residue retention and crop rotation it raises rainfed yields in dry climates, but applying all three principles is often hard for resource-poor smallholders.
basis: Abstract: no-till potential more limited than assumed; with residue retention and rotation, raises rainfed productivity in dry climates; challenging for resource-poor smallholders.

intervention_evidence: Doocy and Tappis 2017, Cash-based approaches in humanitarian emergencies: a systematic review, Campbell Systematic Reviews | Pople, Hill, Dercon and Brunckhorst 2021, Anticipatory Cash Transfers in Climate Disaster Response, CSAE Working Paper
finding: Humanitarian cash and vouchers may improve food security and cost less per beneficiary than in-kind aid, though evidence is low quality; in Bangladesh, cash given ahead of forecast floods cut days without food and later asset losses and costly borrowing.
basis: Doocy abstract: cash may improve food security, lowest cost per beneficiary, low-quality evidence; Pople abstract: pre-flood transfer reduced skipped meals, asset losses, costly borrowing.

intervention_evidence: Samii, Lisiecki, Kulkarni, Paler and Chavis 2014, Effects of decentralized forest management (DFM) on deforestation and poverty in low and middle income countries: a systematic review, Campbell Systematic Reviews
finding: Decentralised forest management in low and middle income countries reduces deforestation, though effects may be modest and the evidence base is small; little research addresses poverty effects, and no study jointly evaluates conservation and poverty outcomes.
basis: Abstract: DFM reduces deforestation, effects may be modest; limited quantity and quality of evidence; little poverty research; no joint conservation-poverty evaluations.

intervention_evidence: Birkenbach, Kaczan and Smith 2017, Catch shares slow the race to fish, Nature
finding: Natural-experiment analysis of 39 US fisheries, each matched to a control, finds catch shares extend fishing seasons and slow the race to fish; the evidence covers US fisheries only.
basis: Abstract: before-after matched comparisons in 39 US fisheries, pooled model and meta-analysis; strong evidence catch shares extend seasons.

intervention_evidence: Geldmann et al. 2013, Effectiveness of terrestrial protected areas in reducing habitat loss and population declines, Biological Conservation
finding: A systematic review finds good evidence that terrestrial protected areas have conserved forest habitat, but evidence that they maintain species populations is inconclusive, and the overall evidence base remains limited.
basis: Abstract: good evidence PAs conserved forest habitat; inconclusive on species populations; positive outcomes but limited evidence base.

intervention_evidence: Snilstveit et al. 2019, Incentives for climate mitigation in the land use sector: the effects of payment for environmental services on environmental and socioeconomic outcomes in low- and middle-income countries: a mixed-methods systematic review, Campbell Systematic Reviews
finding: Payments for environmental services in low and middle income countries may raise household income, reduce deforestation and improve forest cover, but evidence is low quality from few programmes; strong governance and good targeting of sites and participants may raise effectiveness.
basis: Abstract: PES may increase income and reduce deforestation; low and very low quality evidence from few programmes; governance and targeting may improve effectiveness.

intervention_evidence: Assuncao, Gandour and Rocha 2023, DETERring Deforestation in the Amazon: Environmental Monitoring and Law Enforcement, AEJ: Applied Economics | Burgess, Hansen, Olken, Potapov and Sieber 2012, The Political Economy of Deforestation in the Tropics, QJE
finding: In Brazil, satellite deforestation alerts that target field enforcement effectively curbed Amazon clearing; in Indonesia, more political jurisdictions competing over timber increased deforestation, showing that local officials' incentives drive illegal logging.
basis: Assuncao abstract: cloud-cover instrument shows monitoring and enforcement curb deforestation; Burgess abstract: more jurisdictions raise deforestation, officials' incentives matter.

intervention_evidence: Crouzeilles et al. 2016, A global meta-analysis on the ecological drivers of forest restoration success, Nature Communications
finding: Meta-analysis of 221 landscapes finds forest restoration raises biodiversity and vegetation structure above degraded levels but not to full recovery; success grows with time since restoration and is greater where prior disturbance was milder and habitat less fragmented.
basis: Abstract: biodiversity up 15 to 84 percent versus degraded; drivers are time, disturbance type, landscape; restoration does not give full recovery.

intervention_evidence: Jones et al. 2016, Invasive mammal eradication on islands results in substantial conservation gains, PNAS
finding: Across 251 invasive mammal eradications on 181 islands, 236 native species benefited and few were harmed, and several threatened species moved to lower extinction-risk categories; the evidence concerns island eradication, not border biosecurity.
basis: Abstract: literature, database review and expert interviews; 236 species benefited, 7 harmed; four threatened species downlisted; no counterfactual design.

intervention_evidence: Olmstead and Stavins 2009, Comparing price and nonprice approaches to urban water conservation, Water Resources Research | Grafton et al. 2018, The paradox of irrigation efficiency, Science
finding: Reviews argue that pricing urban water cuts demand more cost-effectively than non-price conservation programmes, and that higher irrigation efficiency rarely frees water for other uses unless accompanied by water accounting and a cap on extractions.
basis: Olmstead abstract: prices more cost-effective than non-price programmes; Grafton abstract: efficiency rarely delivers water savings, needs accounting and extraction caps.

intervention_evidence: Ryan and Sudarshan 2022, Rationing the Commons, Journal of Political Economy | Badiani-Magnusson and Jessoe 2019, Electricity Prices, Groundwater, and Agriculture: The Environmental and Agricultural Impacts of Electricity Subsidies in India, NBER chapter in Agricultural Productivity and Producer Behavior
finding: In Rajasthan, rationing farm power held groundwater use near the social optimum on average but misallocated water across farmers, lowering productivity; across India, cheaper agricultural electricity raised groundwater extraction and water-intensive cropping.
basis: Ryan abstract: rationing binds, use near optimal on average, misallocation lowers productivity; Badiani abstract: subsidies increase extraction and water-intensive crop area.

intervention_evidence: Jones, Kondylis, Loeser and Magruder 2022, Factor Market Failures and the Adoption of Irrigation in Rwanda, American Economic Review | Duflo and Pande 2007, Dams, QJE
finding: Free irrigation access in Rwanda raised farm profits sharply, yet farmers irrigated only some plots because of labour costs; in India, large dams raised downstream output and cut downstream poverty but raised poverty in the dam's own district.
basis: Jones abstract: profits up 43 to 62 percent, only 30 percent of plots irrigated due to labour costs; Duflo-Pande abstract: downstream gains, host-district poverty rises.

intervention_evidence: Dinar, Katz, De Stefano and Blankespoor 2019, Do treaties matter? Climate change, water variability, and cooperation along transboundary river basins, Political Geography | Sigman 2002, International Spillovers and Water Quality in Rivers: Do Countries Free Ride?, American Economic Review
finding: Across transboundary basins, a treaty alone shows limited link to cooperation, but more agreements between riparians are robustly associated with cooperation under water variability; international rivers appear more polluted than domestic ones, consistent with free riding, though estimates are sensitive.
basis: Dinar abstract: limited support for treaty effect, number of agreements enhances cooperation; Sigman abstract: free riding may raise pollution, sensitive to country effects.

intervention_evidence: Duflo, Greenstone, Pande and Ryan 2013, Truth-telling by Third-party Auditors and the Response of Polluting Firms: Experimental Evidence from India, QJE | Greenstone and Hanna 2014, Environmental Regulations, Air and Water Pollution, and Infant Mortality in India, American Economic Review
finding: In Gujarat, reforming third-party pollution audits made auditors report truthfully and led treated plants to cut emissions; across India, air pollution regulations substantially improved air quality while water pollution regulations showed no measurable benefit.
basis: Duflo abstract: field experiment, honest reporting, treated plants reduced emissions; Greenstone-Hanna abstract: air regulations improved air quality, water regulations no measurable benefits.

intervention_evidence: Hanna, Duflo and Greenstone 2016, Up in Smoke: The Influence of Household Behavior on the Long-Run Impact of Improved Cooking Stoves, AEJ: Economic Policy | Kremer, Luby, Maertens, Tan and Wiecek 2023, Water Treatment and Child Mortality: A Meta-Analysis and Cost-effectiveness Analysis, NBER Working Paper
finding: Meta-analysis of 52 RCTs finds water treatment cuts under-five mortality by roughly a quarter and is highly cost-effective, while an Indian improved-cookstove trial cut smoke exposure only at first, with no health gains, as household use lapsed.
basis: Kremer abstract: 24 to 27 percent lower odds of under-5 mortality, cost-effective; Hanna abstract: smoke reduction gone by year two, no health effects, irregular use.

intervention_evidence: Blackman 2010, Alternative Pollution Control Policy Instruments in Developing Countries, Review of Environmental Economics and Policy
finding: A review of alternative pollution control tools in developing countries finds no broad convincing evidence that they improve environmental performance; a handful of rigorous studies, mainly of public disclosure, are positive, while many others are negative or inconclusive.
basis: Abstract: handful of rigorous studies, particularly public disclosure, positive; no broad convincing evidence; caution advised on where and how to use tools.

intervention_evidence: Bel and Gradus 2016, Effects of unit-based pricing on household waste collection demand: A meta-regression analysis, Resource and Energy Economics
finding: A meta-analysis of 25 studies of unit-based household waste pricing finds the estimated demand response varies mainly with the pricing system used and whether compostable waste is priced, with no evidence of publication bias.
basis: Abstract: meta-regression of 25 studies on price elasticity; variation tracks pricing system and compostable pricing; bag systems not significant; no publication bias.

intervention_evidence: Andor and Fels 2018, Behavioral economics and energy conservation: a systematic review of non-price interventions and their causal effects, Ecological Economics
finding: A review of 44 causal studies finds social comparisons, commitment devices, goal setting and labelling can meaningfully cut household energy use, but effect sizes vary greatly, so impact evaluations should precede scale-up.
basis: Abstract: 44 studies and 105 treatments with causal designs; all four nudges reduce consumption; effect sizes vary greatly.

intervention_evidence: Sugawara 2014, From Volatility to Stability in Expenditure: Stabilization Funds in Resource-Rich Countries, IMF Working Paper
finding: Across 68 resource-rich countries over 1988 to 2012, government spending volatility was about 13 percent lower where stabilisation funds existed, and political institutions and fiscal rules also reduced volatility; the evidence is cross-country panel association.
basis: Abstract: panel of 68 countries; funds associated with 13 percent lower spending volatility; institutions and fiscal rules significant.

intervention_evidence: Magud and Sosa 2013, When and Why Worry About Real Exchange Rate Appreciation? The Missing Link between Dutch Disease and Growth, Journal of International Commerce, Economics and Policy
finding: A literature review finds resource booms and other inflows appreciate the real exchange rate and shrink manufacturing and net exports, and overvaluation lowers growth, but finds no evidence that Dutch disease reduces overall growth.
basis: Abstract: inflows appreciate RER, reduce manufacturing; overvaluation lowers growth; no evidence Dutch disease reduces growth; does not evaluate exchange-rate management.

intervention_evidence: Rustad, Le Billon and Lujala 2017, Has the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative been a success? Identifying and evaluating EITI goals, Resources Policy
finding: An assessment of EITI against its goals finds it most successful on institutional goals and moderately successful on auditing, reporting and civil society involvement, while its effect on development outcomes remains unresolved.
basis: Abstract: most successful on institutional goals, moderate on operational goals; developmental impact unresolved, partly due to measurement difficulties.

intervention_evidence: Reinhart and Trebesch 2016, Sovereign Debt Relief and Its Aftermath, Journal of the European Economic Association
finding: Across debt crises in 1920 to 1939 and 1978 to 2010, debtor economies improved significantly after debt relief only when it included write-offs; maturity extensions and interest cuts were not generally followed by higher growth or better credit ratings.
basis: Abstract: difference-in-differences around 1934 defaults and Baker and Brady plans; improvement only with write-offs; softer relief not followed by growth.

intervention_evidence: Heinemann, Moessinger and Yeter 2018, Do fiscal rules constrain fiscal policy? A meta-regression-analysis, European Journal of Political Economy
finding: A meta-regression of 30 studies finds fiscal rules appear to constrain fiscal aggregates, but once rule endogeneity and publication bias are accounted for, the effects fall below usual significance levels.
basis: Abstract: 30 studies; constraining effect weakened by endogeneity bias and publication bias, reducing precision below significance.

intervention_evidence: Bova, Ruiz-Arranz, Toscani and Ture 2016, The Fiscal Costs of Contingent Liabilities: A New Dataset, IMF Working Paper
finding: Realised contingent liabilities, averaging about 6 percent of GDP and up to about 40 percent for financial bailouts, are a major source of fiscal distress in advanced and emerging economies; countries with stronger institutions are less exposed.
basis: Abstract: dataset 1990 to 2014; average cost 6 percent of GDP; realisations cluster in crises; stronger institutions less exposed. Measures risk, not disclosure policy.

intervention_evidence: No suitable intervention-level source confirmed

Joshi and Schultz 2013, Family Planning and Women's and Children's Health: Long-Term Consequences of an Outreach Program in Matlab, Bangladesh, Demography | Miller and Babiarz 2016, Family Planning Program Effects: Evidence from Microdata, Population and Development Review
finding: Matlab's family planning and health outreach lowered fertility by about 17 percent and improved birth spacing, child mortality and women's health for two decades; a review of microdata studies finds such programmes explain only a modest share of fertility decline.
basis: Joshi abstract: 17 percent fertility decline, health benefits persisting; Miller-Babiarz abstract: programmes explain 4 to 20 percent of fertility decline, modest welfare effects.

intervention_evidence: Karlan, Ratan and Zinman 2014, Savings by and for the Poor: A Research Review and Agenda, Review of Income and Wealth | Dupas, Karlan, Robinson and Ubfal 2018, Banking the Unbanked? Evidence from Three Countries, AEJ: Applied Economics
finding: Transaction costs, mistrust, information gaps, social constraints and behavioural biases hold back poor people's saving; in Uganda, Malawi and Chile, offering basic bank accounts led few to use them actively and had no average effect on savings or later outcomes.
basis: Karlan abstract: five constraint sets reviewed with field experiments; Dupas abstract: few active users, no intention-to-treat effects on savings or downstream outcomes.

intervention_evidence: Staubli and Zweimuller 2013, Does raising the early retirement age increase employment of older workers?, Journal of Public Economics
finding: Raising Austria's early retirement age raised employment of affected older workers, but also substantially raised unemployment claims; gains were largest for higher-wage, healthier workers, while others bridged through unemployment or disability benefits.
basis: Abstract: ERA raised from 60 to 62 for men; employment up 9.75 points; large unemployment insurance spillovers; responses largest for high-wage, healthy workers.

intervention_evidence: Fu, Noguchi, Kawamura, Takahashi and Tamiya 2017, Spillover effect of Japanese long-term care insurance as an employment promotion policy for family caregivers, Journal of Health Economics
finding: Introducing Japan's public long-term care insurance had significant positive spillover effects on family caregivers' labour force participation, varying by gender and age, while a later amendment had generally negative spillovers.
basis: Abstract: difference-in-difference propensity score matching on 1995 to 2013 national data; introduction positive spillovers, amendment negative.

intervention_evidence: Lederman, Olarreaga and Payton 2010, Export promotion agencies: Do they work?, Journal of Development Economics
finding: Using survey data on export promotion agencies in 103 countries, agencies are associated with significantly higher exports on average, with strong diminishing returns to agency budgets.
basis: Abstract: survey of agencies in 103 countries; statistically significant effect on exports on average; strong diminishing returns.

intervention_evidence: Donaldson 2018, Railroads of the Raj: Estimating the Impact of Transportation Infrastructure, American Economic Review | Cosar and Demir 2016, Domestic road infrastructure and international trade: Evidence from Turkey, Journal of Development Economics
finding: Railroads in colonial India cut trade costs and regional price gaps and raised trade and real incomes; in Turkey, expressway upgrades sharply lowered shipment costs, with larger gains for time-sensitive industries in provinces' international trade.
basis: Donaldson abstract: railroads lowered trade costs, raised trade and real incomes; Cosar-Demir abstract: expressway shipments 70 percent cheaper, more for time-sensitive industries.

intervention_evidence: Fernandes, Hillberry and Mendoza Alcantara 2021, Trade Effects of Customs Reform: Evidence from Albania, World Bank Economic Review
finding: Albania's customs reform that sharply cut physical inspections of imports raised imports, most for the least frequently observed flows, largely independently of clearance time, with no clear rise in evasion.
basis: Abstract: reduced inspections significantly increase imports, largest in least observed flows; effect largely independent of clearance time; no clear evasion increase.

intervention_evidence: Campante and Yanagizawa-Drott 2018, Long-Range Growth: Economic Development in the Global Network of Air Links, QJE | Giroud 2013, Proximity and Investment: Evidence from Plant-Level Data, QJE
finding: Long-distance air links raised local economic activity and business links worldwide, with capital flowing mostly from high- to middle-income countries; in the US, new routes cutting headquarters-to-plant travel raised plant investment and productivity.
basis: Campante abstract: 6,000-mile discontinuity, night lights and business links rise; Giroud abstract: new routes raise plant investment 8 to 9 percent and productivity.

intervention_evidence: Cipollina and Salvatici 2010, Reciprocal Trade Agreements in Gravity Models: A Meta-Analysis, Review of International Economics
finding: A meta-analysis of gravity-model estimates robustly rejects the hypothesis that reciprocal trade agreements have no effect on members' trade, while estimates vary widely with data, specification and publication selection.
basis: Abstract: pooled fixed and random effects estimates; no-effect hypothesis robustly rejected; sensitivity to specifications and publication selection tested.

intervention_evidence: Winters, McCulloch and McKay 2004, Trade Liberalization and Poverty: The Evidence So Far, Journal of Economic Literature
finding: A review finds no simple general link between trade liberalisation and poverty in developing countries: in the long run and on average it is likely strongly poverty alleviating, but the poor may be less able to cope with short-run adverse effects.
basis: Abstract: no simple generalizable conclusion; long-run average likely poverty alleviating; poor less placed to protect themselves in the short run.

intervention_evidence: Faber and Gaubert 2019, Tourism and Economic Development: Evidence from Mexico's Coastline, American Economic Review
finding: In Mexico, tourism caused large local economic gains, partly by boosting nearby manufacturing, but these were largely offset nationally by weaker agglomeration in less touristic regions; the study does not evaluate destination development programmes.
basis: Abstract: large local gains relative to less touristic regions; spillovers largely offset by lost agglomeration elsewhere; national gains mainly from market integration.

intervention_evidence: Ekin, Ekin, Akbulut and Celik 2026, Carrying Capacity and Adaptive Visitor Use Management for Sustainable Parks and Protected Recreation Areas: A Critical Narrative Review, Sustainability
finding: A narrative review of carrying capacity in parks and protected recreation areas concludes that sustainable management depends more on implementing an indicator, standard, monitoring and action chain than on a numerical visitor limit; it presents no outcome evidence.
basis: Abstract: carrying capacity is an adaptive process, not a visitor count; management depends on indicator-standard-monitoring-action chain; claims are conceptual, not tested.

intervention_evidence: No suitable intervention-level source confirmed

Alfaro-Urena, Manelici and Vasquez 2022, The Effects of Joining Multinational Supply Chains: New Evidence from Firm-to-Firm Linkages, QJE | Atkin, Khandelwal and Osman 2017, Exporting and Firm Performance: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment, QJE
finding: Costa Rican firms that began supplying multinationals had 26 percent more workers and higher productivity four years on; in Egypt, randomly offered export orders raised rug producers' profits and quality through learning by exporting.
basis: Alfaro-Urena abstract: employment up 26 percent, TFP up 4 to 9 percent; Atkin abstract: randomized export access raised profits and quality, learning-by-exporting.

intervention_evidence: Harrison and Rodriguez-Clare 2010, Trade, Foreign Investment, and Industrial Policy for Developing Countries, Handbook of Development Economics
finding: A review of theory and evidence finds no support for hard industrial policies that distort prices to capture externalities, but sees a role for soft industrial policy in which government and private groups collaborate to raise cluster productivity.
basis: Abstract: no support for hard price-distorting interventions; role for soft industrial policy via public-private collaboration, skills, technology adoption, infrastructure.

intervention_evidence: Lane 2025, Manufacturing Revolutions: Industrial Policy and Industrialization in South Korea, QJE
finding: South Korea's 1973 to 1979 heavy and chemical industry drive expanded directly targeted industries and their dynamic comparative advantage, benefited downstream users, and had effects that lasted after the policy ended.
basis: Abstract: HCI policies promoted expansion and dynamic comparative advantage of targeted industries; downstream benefits; persistent effects after policy end.

intervention_evidence: Jensen 2012, Do Labor Market Opportunities Affect Young Women's Work and Family Decisions? Experimental Evidence from India, QJE
finding: In rural India, randomly provided recruiting services for business process outsourcing jobs led young women to delay marriage and childbearing and pursue work or training; it shows effects of services job opportunities, not of policies that build the sector.
basis: Abstract: randomized BPO recruiting in villages; women less likely to marry or have children, more work, schooling or training.

intervention_evidence: Dimos and Pugh 2016, The effectiveness of R&D subsidies: A meta-regression analysis of the evaluation literature, Research Policy
finding: A meta-regression of 52 micro-level evaluations since 2000 rejects crowding out of private R&D by public subsidies but finds no evidence of substantial additionality.
basis: Abstract: 52 studies; after controlling for publication bias, crowding out rejected and no substantial additionality found.

intervention_evidence: Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie and Roberts 2013, Does Management Matter? Evidence from India, QJE
finding: Free management consulting for randomly chosen large Indian textile firms raised productivity by 17 percent in the first year; firms had not adopted the practices mainly because of informational barriers.
basis: Abstract: field experiment; productivity up 17 percent in first year; informational barriers primary reason for non-adoption.

intervention_evidence: Branstetter, Fisman and Foley 2006, Do Stronger Intellectual Property Rights Increase International Technology Transfer? Empirical Evidence from U.S. Firm-Level Panel Data, QJE
finding: After patent reforms in sixteen countries, US multinationals raised royalty payments, affiliate R&D and foreign patent applications there, concentrated among parents that relied heavily on US patents.
basis: Abstract: royalties, affiliate R&D and patent applications rise at reforms; increases concentrated among patent-intensive parents, royalties up over 30 percent.

intervention_evidence: Hvide and Jones 2018, University Innovation and the Professor's Privilege, American Economic Review | de Negri, Lemos and de Negri 2006, The Impact of University Enterprise Incentive Program on the Performance and Technological Efforts of Brazilian Industrial Firms, IDB Office of Evaluation and Oversight Working Paper OVE/WP-13/06
finding: Ending Norway's professor's privilege, which moved invention rights to universities, roughly halved researcher start-ups and patenting. In Brazil, grants for joint university-firm projects raised firms' private R&D spending, but effects on firm growth and productivity were inconclusive.
basis: Hvide-Jones abstract: start-ups and patents fell about half after reform; de Negri: matching shows higher private R&D, no significant growth difference.

intervention_evidence: Kantor and Whalley 2023, Moonshot: Public R&D and Growth, NBER Working Paper 31471 | Gross and Sampat 2023, America, Jump-Started: World War II R&D and the Takeoff of the US Innovation System, American Economic Review
finding: US Cold War space R&D raised manufacturing output, employment and investment in space-related industries, but its overall economic effects were modest; World War II applied R&D seeded lasting US technology clusters and high-tech entrepreneurship. Evidence is from the United States only.
basis: Kantor-Whalley abstract: NASA contractor R&D raised output in related industries, modest overall; Gross-Sampat abstract: OSRD created clusters lasting into the 1970s.

intervention_evidence: Alston, Chan-Kang, Marra, Pardey and Wyatt 2000, A Meta-Analysis of Rates of Return to Agricultural R&D: Ex Pede Herculem?, IFPRI Research Report 113 | Renkow and Byerlee 2010, The impacts of CGIAR research: A review of recent evidence, Food Policy
finding: A meta-analysis of reported returns to agricultural research finds high but debated rates with systematic biases; a review of CGIAR evidence finds strongly positive impacts relative to investment, largest for crop genetic improvement, while resource-management and policy research benefits are more local.
basis: Alston abstract: reported returns typically high, credibility debated, biases identified; Renkow-Byerlee abstract: strongly positive impacts, crop improvement most documented.

intervention_evidence: Crescenzi, Di Cataldo and Giua 2021, FDI inflows in Europe: Does investment promotion work?, Journal of International Economics | Klemm and Van Parys 2012, Empirical evidence on the effects of tax incentives, International Tax and Public Finance
finding: Investment promotion agencies raise FDI inflows even in European economies, most in less developed regions, knowledge-intensive sectors and for inexperienced investors; in developing countries, lower tax rates and longer tax holidays attract FDI but not total private investment or growth.
basis: Crescenzi abstract: IPA effects largest in less developed areas and for occasional investors; Klemm abstract: tax holidays attract FDI, no effect on capital formation or growth.

intervention_evidence: Havranek and Irsova 2011, Estimating vertical spillovers from FDI: Why results vary and what the true effect is, Journal of International Economics | Alfaro-Urena, Manelici and Vasquez 2022, The Effects of Joining Multinational Supply Chains: New Evidence from Firm-to-Firm Linkages, Quarterly Journal of Economics
